topic: Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026

subtopics.title: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 and the 2026 Bill
subtopics.summary: The 1971 Act makes insult to the National Flag and Constitution, and preventing the singing of the National Anthem, punishable offences. The Central Government has introduced an amendment in the Rajya Sabha to bring Vande Mataram under similar statutory protection. The Bill proposes imprisonment up to 3 years, fine or both for intentionally insulting the song.
facts: Section 2 prohibits intentional insult to or disrespect for the National Flag and Constitution.
Examples under Section 2 include burning, defacing, desecrating or showing disrespect.
Section 3 prohibits intentionally preventing the singing of the National Anthem.
Section 3 also prohibits causing disturbance to an assembly during its singing.
Sections 2 and 3 each carry up to 3 years' imprisonment, fine or both.
Section 3A was inserted through the 2003 Amendment.
Section 3A prescribes a minimum 1 year imprisonment for second and subsequent convictions under Sections 2 or 3.
The Bill seeks to extend statutory protection to Vande Mataram, similar to that for the National Anthem.
Under the Bill, intentionally insulting Vande Mataram would be punishable.
Proposed Bill punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years, fine or both.

subtopics.title: Vande Mataram: origin and early history
subtopics.summary: Vande Mataram was written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay as a patriotic response to British promotion of 'God Save the King/Queen'. It was written on 7 November 1875 in the magazine Bangadarshan and published in the novel Anandamath in 1882. It became a rallying cry of the Swadeshi Movement after the Partition of Bengal in 1905.
facts: Author: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay.
Composed as a patriotic response to British promotion of 'God Save the King/Queen'.
Written on 7 November 1875 in the magazine Bangadarshan.
Published in 1882 in the Bengali novel Anandamath.
Structure: 6 stanzas; first two in Sanskrit, last four in Bengali.
Rabindranath Tagore sang it at the 1896 INC Session in Calcutta.
Became the customary opening song at the Varanasi Congress Session (1905), sung by Sarala Devi Chaudhurani.
First public use: 7 August 1905 at Town Hall, Calcutta.
Became the rallying cry of the Swadeshi Movement after the Partition of Bengal (1905).
In 1907, Bhikaji Cama unfurled an Indian flag at Stuttgart with the song inscribed.

subtopics.title: National Song vs National Anthem and constitutional status
subtopics.summary: Dr. Rajendra Prasad declared Vande Mataram the National Song of India on 24 January 1950, with only its first two stanzas officially recognised. Jana Gana Mana was adopted as the National Anthem the same day, with the entire anthem officially recognised, and is already protected under the 1971 Act. The Constitution does not explicitly recognise a National Song.
facts: 24 January 1950: Dr. Rajendra Prasad declared Vande Mataram the National Song of India.
Vande Mataram is to be honoured equally with the National Anthem.
Only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram have official recognition.
1937 Congress Working Committee decision: only the first two stanzas to be used for national gatherings.
Jana Gana Mana was adopted as the National Anthem on 24 January 1950, with the entire anthem officially recognised.
Jana Gana Mana is already protected under the 1971 Act.
The Constitution does not explicitly recognise a National Song.
Article 51A(a): Fundamental Duties require citizens to respect the National Flag and National Anthem.
Parliamentary protocol: sessions open with the National Anthem and close (sine die) with Vande Mataram.

quizzes.passage:
India protects its national symbols through specific laws. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, is the main law that deals with deliberate insults to the national emblems. It covers the National Flag, the Constitution and the National Anthem, Jana Gana Mana, and it makes certain acts against them punishable. The law describes acts such as burning, defacing or desecrating the flag, and it also covers preventing people from singing the anthem or disturbing a gathering while it is sung. The Act has three main provisions, dealing with the flag and Constitution, the anthem, and repeat offences. The Act was later strengthened so that people who repeat such offences face stricter treatment.

In 2026, the Central Government proposed an amendment to this law in the Rajya Sabha. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, aims to extend statutory protection to Vande Mataram, a patriotic song. Under the proposal, intentionally insulting Vande Mataram would become a punishable offence. At present, the Act protects the flag, the Constitution and the anthem, while the amendment seeks to include the National Song, Vande Mataram, within this legal framework. Both the law and the proposed amendment concern national honour.

quizzes.passage:
Vande Mataram is a patriotic song written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. It was composed as a response to British promotion of 'God Save the King', and it first appeared in a magazine in 1875. Later, the song became part of a novel in which warrior-monks sing it. The song praises Mother India through the image of a goddess, and its verses are divided into stanzas, with some verses in Sanskrit and the rest in Bengali.

After the Partition of Bengal in 1905, the song became closely linked with the national struggle. It was sung in public for the first time at Town Hall in Calcutta, and it soon became the customary opening song at a Congress session. An Indian flag bearing its words was also unfurled in Europe. Several tunes were composed for the song over the years, and it was sung at many national events.

Later, the national leadership had to decide how much of the song should be used at gatherings. After independence, the song was declared the National Song of India and was to be honoured equally with the National Anthem. The Constitution does not explicitly recognise a National Song. Its popularity and its official status therefore developed over several decades.
